title: Sequences, mappings and sets
summary: Lists, tuples, dicts and sets are not four interchangeable containers. Each one makes a different operation cheap, and choosing the wrong one is the most common reason correct Python is slow. The choice is driven by two questions: what do you look things up by, and does the collection change?
definition: A sequence stores items in positional order and is indexed by integer position (`list`, `tuple`, `str`, `range`). A mapping stores key-to-value pairs and is indexed by hashable key (`dict`). A set stores unique hashable items with no positional order and answers membership. All three share the iteration protocol and the `in` operator, which is what makes them look more alike than they are.
purpose: Once a collection holds more than a few hundred items, the container choice dominates everything else you do. `x in some_list` walks the whole list; `x in some_set` hashes once. Both are one line, both are correct, and one of them turns a nested loop from O(n²) into O(n). You learn the container model so that the fast version is the one you reach for by default, and so that `TypeError: unhashable type` reads as information rather than an obstacle.

body.md:
Start from what each container is *for*, not from its syntax:

- **`list`** — an ordered, mutable, growable sequence. Reach for it when position matters or when you are accumulating results. Appending is amortised O(1); inserting at the front is O(n) because every element shifts.
- **`tuple`** — an immutable sequence, and therefore hashable if its contents are. Reach for it for a fixed-shape record (`(lat, lon)`), for a dict key made of several parts, and for anything you want to be unable to modify.
- **`dict`** — a mapping from hashable key to value with O(1) average lookup, insertion and deletion. Since 3.7 it preserves insertion order as a language guarantee, so it doubles as an ordered set of keys.
- **`set`** / **`frozenset`** — unordered unique membership with O(1) average `in`, plus real set algebra (`|`, `&`, `-`, `^`). Reach for it the moment you find yourself asking "have I seen this already?"

The decision is rarely aesthetic. If your lookups are by identity or key, a list is the wrong container no matter how natural it feels to build one.

body.title: `in` on a list is the quiet quadratic
body.md:
```python
# O(n * m): for every row, walk the whole blocklist
kept = [r for r in rows if r.id not in blocked_ids]     # blocked_ids is a list

# O(n + m): hash once per row
blocked = set(blocked_ids)
kept = [r for r in rows if r.id not in blocked]
```

This is the single highest-yield performance fix in most Python codebases, and it is invisible in review because both versions read identically. The tell is a membership test inside a loop against a container built elsewhere.

Hashability is the rule that decides what may be a dict key or a set member. An object is hashable if it has a `__hash__` that stays constant for its lifetime and an `__eq__` consistent with it. Immutable built-ins qualify; `list`, `dict` and `set` deliberately do not, because a key whose hash changed after insertion would be unfindable — it would sit in the wrong bucket forever.

That is why `d[[1, 2]]` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` and `d[(1, 2)]` works. It is also why a mutable class you give a `__hash__` to must not let the hashed fields change; the standard resolution is to hash a tuple of the fields and freeze them.

body.caption: Idioms worth having in your fingers
body.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

rows = [("eu", 3), ("us", 5), ("eu", 2)]

# Group without pre-seeding keys.
by_region = defaultdict(list)
for region, value in rows:
    by_region[region].append(value)
print(dict(by_region))

# Count without a manual +1 dance.
print(Counter(region for region, _ in rows).most_common(1))

# Read with a default instead of a KeyError.
print({"a": 1}.get("b", 0))

# Dedupe while preserving first-seen order: dict keys are ordered.
print(list(dict.fromkeys([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])))

# A FIFO queue. list.pop(0) is O(n); deque.popleft is O(1).
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.appendleft(0)
print(q.popleft(), list(q))

body.title: Picking a container in four questions
steps: What do I look items up by? Position → list/tuple. A key → dict. Presence only → set.
Does it change after construction? No → tuple or frozenset, which are also hashable and safe to share.
Do I need uniqueness? Yes → set, or `dict.fromkeys` when you also need to keep order.
Am I adding or removing at the front? Yes → `collections.deque`, never a list.

body.definition_md: `d.keys()`, `d.values()` and `d.items()` return dynamic views, not copies: they reflect later changes to the dict and support set operations (`d1.keys() & d2.keys()`). Because they are live, mutating a dict while iterating a view raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` — iterate `list(d)` when you intend to delete.

body.title: Memory is part of the choice
body.md:
A dict costs roughly two to three times a list of the same number of items, because it stores hashes and keys alongside values. At a few thousand entries that is irrelevant; at ten million it decides whether the process fits in its container limit.

When you are holding many small fixed-shape records, a list of tuples or `__slots__` objects is dramatically cheaper than a list of dicts — the per-record key strings are interned but the per-record table is not. Measure with `sys.getsizeof` plus the contents, or `tracemalloc`, before assuming.

components.name: hashable key
components.role: Immutable, consistent `__hash__`/`__eq__`. The entry requirement for dict keys and set members.

components.name: iteration protocol
components.role: `__iter__` is what makes all four containers interchangeable in a `for` loop and a comprehension.

components.name: collections module
components.role: `defaultdict`, `Counter`, `deque`, `namedtuple` — the specialised containers that remove hand-rolled bookkeeping.

common_errors.error: `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` when using a list as a dict key or putting it in a set.
common_errors.cause: Lists are mutable, so their hash could change after insertion and the entry would become unreachable. Python refuses rather than corrupt the table.
common_errors.fix: Convert to a `tuple` (or `frozenset` when order does not matter): `seen.add(tuple(row))`.

common_errors.cause: `for k in d:` iterates a live view; deleting during the loop invalidates it.
common_errors.fix: Iterate a snapshot — `for k in list(d):` — or build the survivors with a comprehension and rebind.

common_errors.error: A nested loop that was fast in testing takes minutes in production.
common_errors.cause: An `in` against a list inside a loop: O(n·m) growth that only shows up once both collections are real.
common_errors.fix: Hoist the inner container into a `set` (or dict) once, outside the loop.

common_errors.error: `d[key]` raises `KeyError` on data that is legitimately optional.
common_errors.cause: Subscripting asserts the key exists; that is the right behaviour for a required field and the wrong one for an optional field.
common_errors.fix: `d.get(key)`, `d.get(key, default)`, or `d.setdefault(key, [])` when you are about to append. Use `defaultdict` when every access should auto-create.

common_errors.error: Two lists of the same items compare unequal, or a `set` comparison surprises you.
common_errors.cause: Sequence equality is order-sensitive; set equality is not.
common_errors.fix: Compare `set(a) == set(b)` for 'same members', `sorted(a) == sorted(b)` for 'same multiset', and `a == b` only when order is part of the contract.

common_errors.error: `d = dict.fromkeys(keys, [])` produces one list shared by every key.
common_errors.cause: The default value is evaluated once and the same object is stored under every key — the mutable-default problem in a different costume.
common_errors.fix: `defaultdict(list)`, or `{k: [] for k in keys}` which evaluates the literal per key.

best_practices: Convert to a `set` before any membership test that runs inside a loop; do it once, outside the loop.
Use `tuple` for fixed-shape records and composite dict keys — immutability is what makes them hashable and safe to share.
Prefer `defaultdict` and `Counter` over hand-written 'if key not in d' bookkeeping; they are faster and remove a class of bug.
Use `dict.fromkeys(items)` to dedupe while keeping first-seen order, rather than a set plus a manual order list.
Reach for `collections.deque` for any queue; `list.pop(0)` is O(n) and silently degrades as the queue grows.
Iterate `list(d)` whenever the loop body may add or remove keys, and prefer rebuilding over in-place deletion.
production_considerations: Container choice is usually a bigger performance lever than algorithmic cleverness: one list-to-set change routinely beats a rewrite.
Dicts cost 2-3x the memory of an equivalent list of tuples; at multi-million scale that is the difference between fitting in RAM and swapping.
Dict insertion order is guaranteed and is therefore safe to depend on for reproducible output — but relying on it in a public API silently forbids you from ever switching to a set.

Sets and dicts have O(n) worst-case lookup under adversarial hash collisions. Python's string hash randomisation (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) exists to make that unreachable from untrusted input; never disable it in a service.
`in` on a generator consumes it. Testing membership twice against the same generator silently returns false the second time — materialise it first.
anti_patterns: Building a list purely to answer membership questions against it.
`list.pop(0)` in a queue loop, or `list.insert(0, x)` in an accumulation loop.
Using a dict keyed by integers `0..n-1` where a list was the container being described.
`sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[0])` to restore an order the dict already preserved.
Mutating a dict or set inside a `for` loop over itself.

examples.title: The list-to-set fix, measured
examples.code:
import timeit

blocked = list(range(20_000))
rows = list(range(20_000))

slow = timeit.timeit(lambda: [r for r in rows if r not in blocked], number=1)
fast_set = set(blocked)
fast = timeit.timeit(lambda: [r for r in rows if r not in fast_set], number=1)
print(f"list: {slow:.3f}s  set: {fast:.4f}s")
